group.title: Precise verbs
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: To collect information slowly and with effort, often bit by bit.
examples: We {gleaned} a few useful facts from the old letters.
wrong: She gleaned the details by refusing to read anything.

words.meaning: To say officially that something you said earlier was not true.
examples: The paper {retracted} the false story.
wrong: He retracted his claim by repeating it even louder.

words.meaning: To tell someone formally that they did something wrong.
examples: The officer was {reprimanded} for being late.
wrong: The boss reprimanded her by praising her excellent work.

words.meaning: To praise someone formally or in public.
examples: The mayor {commended} the firefighters for their bravery.
wrong: He commended the team by criticizing everything they did.

words.meaning: To escape or avoid something, often in a dishonest way.
examples: He {evaded} the question by changing the subject.
wrong: She evaded the question by answering it fully and directly.

words.meaning: To invent false facts or stories to trick people.
examples: The witness {fabricated} evidence.
wrong: He fabricated the data by recording exactly what happened.

words.meaning: To lose strength or confidence and start to fail.
examples: Her voice {faltered} as she spoke.
wrong: The economy faltered, growing strongly and steadily.

words.meaning: To lose something as a punishment or because you broke a rule.
examples: The team {forfeited} the match after arriving late.
wrong: They forfeited the prize, so they got to keep it.

words.meaning: To control and use something for a useful purpose.
examples: The dam {harnesses} the river to make electricity.
wrong: They harnessed the wind’s power by letting it go to waste.

words.meaning: To collect and hide large amounts of something.
examples: People {hoarded} food before the storm.
wrong: He hoarded money by giving it all away.

words.meaning: To make someone suffer something bad or painful.
examples: The storm {inflicted} heavy damage on the coast.
wrong: The medicine inflicted relief and comfort on the patient.

words.meaning: To slowly make someone have a feeling or idea.
examples: Good coaches {instill} confidence in their players.
wrong: She instilled discipline by never setting any rules.

words.meaning: To put something in danger of being harmed or lost.
examples: One mistake could {jeopardize} the whole project.
wrong: He jeopardized his job by doing it perfectly.

words.meaning: To persuade someone to go somewhere or do something by offering something attractive.
examples: Low prices {lured} shoppers into the store.
wrong: The ads lured customers away by making the shop look awful.

words.meaning: To block a path or stop something from happening.
examples: A fallen tree {obstructed} the road.
wrong: The barrier obstructed traffic by letting every car through.

words.meaning: To make it harder for something to happen or move forward.
examples: Heavy snow {hampered} the rescue effort.
wrong: The good weather hampered the rescue by making it quick and easy.

words.meaning: To say formally that you no longer accept or want something.
examples: He {renounced} his title to marry her.
wrong: She renounced her citizenship by proudly keeping it.

words.meaning: To pay attention to advice or a warning and act on it.
examples: Hikers who {heed} the warnings stay safe.
wrong: He heeded my advice by doing the exact opposite.

words.meaning: To do something harmful to someone because they harmed you.
examples: The country {retaliated} with its own taxes on imports.
wrong: He retaliated by thanking them warmly for the insult.

words.meaning: To save something from being destroyed or ruined.
examples: They managed to {salvage} the deal at the last minute.
wrong: The crew salvaged the cargo by letting it sink.

words.meaning: To ask for something such as money, help or opinions.
examples: The council is {soliciting} feedback from residents.
wrong: They solicited opinions by refusing to listen to anyone.

words.meaning: To state clearly that something must be done as part of an agreement.
examples: The contract {stipulates} payment within thirty days.
wrong: The rules stipulate nothing, so everything is clearly required.

words.meaning: To damage something so it works less well.
examples: Lack of sleep can {impair} your judgment.
wrong: The loud noise impaired her hearing, making it sharper than ever.

words.meaning: To stop someone from doing what they planned.
examples: Police {thwarted} the robbery.
wrong: The guards thwarted the escape by opening every door.

words.meaning: To picture a future situation or plan in your mind.
examples: I {envisage} a much larger company in five years.
wrong: She envisaged the future without imagining anything at all.

words.meaning: To choose not to demand something you have a right to.
examples: The bank {waived} the fee this month.
wrong: They waived the fee, so we had to pay it twice.

words.meaning: To refuse to give something.
examples: The company {withheld} payment until the work was finished.
wrong: She withheld the information by telling everyone.

words.meaning: To force someone to do something.
examples: The rain {compelled} us to cancel the game.
wrong: Nothing compelled him, so he was forced to go.

words.meaning: To cause a state or feeling, or persuade someone to do something.
examples: The warm room and soft music {induced} sleep.
wrong: The strong coffee induced sleep and kept him wide awake.

words.meaning: To consider or judge something in a particular way.
examples: The building was {deemed} unsafe.
wrong: The plan was deemed, so nobody formed any opinion about it.

words.meaning: To formally give an honor, gift or right to someone.
examples: The king {bestowed} a medal on the soldier.
wrong: The university bestowed a degree on her by taking it away.

words.meaning: To speak to someone sharply because they did something wrong.
examples: The coach {rebuked} the players for their lazy effort.
wrong: She rebuked him warmly for his excellent work.

words.meaning: To invent a plan or method using careful thought.
examples: Engineers {devised} a new cooling system.
wrong: She devised a plan by copying one without any thought.

words.meaning: To make a feeling or belief go away.
examples: The report {dispelled} fears about job losses.
wrong: His kind words dispelled her worries and made them stronger.

words.meaning: To change facts or information so that they are no longer true.
examples: The article {distorted} what the minister said.
wrong: He distorted the facts by reporting them exactly.

words.meaning: To make something change direction or be used for another purpose.
examples: Traffic was {diverted} around the accident.
wrong: The funds were diverted, so they went exactly where planned.

words.meaning: To be a perfect example of an idea or quality.
examples: She {embodies} the spirit of the team.
wrong: He embodies honesty, as he lies all the time.

words.meaning: To include many different things.
examples: The course {encompasses} history, art and politics.
wrong: The program encompasses everything, so it leaves most topics out.

words.meaning: To involve something as a necessary part or result.
examples: The job {entails} a lot of travel.
wrong: The role entails travel, so you never have to leave town.

words.meaning: To use power, influence or effort to make something happen.
examples: Parents {exert} a strong influence on children.
wrong: She exerted great effort by sitting back and doing nothing.
